sections.preamble:
\section*{\texorpdfstring{Polynomial-Time P-Matrix Linear Complementarity Problem}{Polynomial-Time P-Matrix Linear Complementarity Problem}}\label{424}

\subsection{Definitions and mathematical statement}
A real square matrix $M$ is a $P$-matrix if every principal minor is strictly positive. For rational $M\in{\mathbb{Q}}^{n\times n}$ and $q\in{\mathbb{Q}}^n$, a linear complementarity solution consists of vectors $z,w\in{\mathbb{R}}^n$ with
\[
 w=Mz+q,\qquad z\ge0,\quad w\ge0,\quad z^{\mathsf T}w=0.
\]
The last condition is equivalent to $z_iw_i=0$ for all $i$. For a $P$-matrix the solution is unique. The task asks for a deterministic algorithm computing this solution in time polynomial in the binary encoding length of $(M,q)$, under the promise that $M$ is a $P$-matrix. Recognizing that promise is a separate problem. Arithmetic-operation counts with unbounded real precision do not establish a bit-complexity bound.
\par\smallskip\textit{Formulation and concept references:} \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.08992}{[S1]}.

\subsection{Short English statement}
Can the unique solution of every rational $P$-matrix linear complementarity problem be found in polynomial bit time?

\subsection{Research attempt}
\paragraph{Scope, process, and first gap.}
This GPT-6 Astra Ultra attempt, dated 27 September 2026, studies complementary supports and exact rational arithmetic. It proves a polynomial output-size bound, an exponential finite search, and a polynomial-time triangular subcase, then tests a simultaneous iteration on an explicit $P$-matrix. These are standard partial arguments. The promise is retained and is never replaced by a procedure for recognizing $P$-matrices.

The source [S1] distinguishes general geometric unique-sink orientations from additional structure arising in symmetric complementarity problems. Its symmetric results cannot be applied to every nonsymmetric $P$-matrix. The first gap here is finding a feasible complementary support in polynomial time; the rational numbers describing a solution do not themselves require exponentially many bits.

\paragraph{A support determines a rational candidate.}
For a subset $S\subseteq[n]$, impose
\[
 z_{[n]\setminus S}=0,\qquad w_S=0.
\]
Every principal submatrix $M_{SS}$ is invertible by the $P$-matrix promise. Thus the resulting candidate is uniquely determined:
\[
 z_S=-M_{SS}^{-1}q_S,\qquad w=Mz+q.
 \tag{424.1}
\]
Check $z\ge0$ and $w\ge0$ exactly. If both hold, the imposed equations make every product $z_iw_i$ zero, so this is a solution.

Conversely, take the unique solution guaranteed by the promise and let $S=\{i:z_i>0\}$. Complementarity gives $w_S=0$, so it is obtained by (424.1). Enumerating all $2^n$ subsets therefore finds a solution. The empty subset is included: it gives $z=0,w=q$, valid when $q\ge0$.

Degeneracy causes no gap. If both $z_i$ and $w_i$ vanish, several subsets may produce the same solution. The promise says that valid solution vectors are unique, not that their combinatorial support certificates must be unique. Requiring every coordinate indexed by $S$ to be strictly positive would be unnecessary for the verification test.

\paragraph{Polynomial bit length of the output.}
Let $L$ be the total binary input length. Multiply $M$ and $q$ by the product $D>0$ of their denominators. This product has $O(L)$ bits. We obtain an integer matrix $A=DM$ and integer vector $b=Dq$ whose entries also have $O(L)$ bits, and the candidate equations are
\[
 A_{SS}z_S=-b_S.
\]
Cramer's rule expresses each coordinate as a ratio of determinants of order at most $n$. The determinant expansion, or Hadamard's inequality, bounds their bit lengths by $O(nL+n\log n)$. Computing $w=(Az+b)/D$ also gives a polynomial-size rational vector.

Thus every promised input has a rational solution of polynomial encoding length. For a supplied support, fraction-free elimination and exact sign tests run in polynomial bit time; the relevant intermediate determinants satisfy the same size bound. Listing $2^n$ supports remains exponential. A short verifiable answer does not explain how to locate its support quickly.

This distinction also prevents an unjustified complexity-class conclusion about unpromised inputs. Verification of the displayed rational equations is easy, but the total-solvability guarantee used here assumes that $M$ is a $P$-matrix. No recognition algorithm or total search procedure outside that promise has been proved.

\paragraph{An exact triangular algorithm.}
Suppose $M$ is lower triangular with positive diagonal. Every principal submatrix is lower triangular with positive diagonal product, so this is indeed a $P$-matrix subclass. Process coordinates in order. Once $z_1,\ldots,z_{i-1}$ are known, set
\[
 a_i=q_i+\sum_{j<i}M_{ij}z_j.
\]
The remaining coordinate equation is $w_i=M_{ii}z_i+a_i$. Its unique nonnegative complementary solution is
\[
 z_i=\max\{0,-a_i/M_{ii}\},\qquad
 w_i=\max\{0,a_i\}.
 \tag{424.2}
\]
If $a_i\ge0$, positive $z_i$ would make $w_i>0$, violating complementarity, so $z_i=0$. If $a_i<0$, nonnegativity of $w_i$ requires $z_i>0$, and then complementarity forces $w_i=0$. This proves (424.2), including $a_i=0$. Induction proves the whole solution.

There are $O(n^2)$ arithmetic operations, but a bit bound is also needed. Use the cleared integer data $A,b$. At step $i$, all denominators divide $\prod_{j\le i}A_{jj}$, whose bit length is $O(nL)$. Since the positive integer diagonals are at least one, a rough recurrence bounds magnitudes by $(1+2^{O(L)})^{O(n)}$. Numerators therefore also have polynomial bit length. Ordinary exact arithmetic implements the recurrence in polynomial bit time.

An upper triangular matrix is handled in reverse order, and a known simultaneous row/column permutation to triangular form is handled by relabeling coordinates. The proof uses this acyclic dependency order essentially.

\paragraph{Why a convexity shortcut changes the matrix.}
For a symmetric positive definite matrix, the complementarity conditions are the optimality conditions of minimizing
\[
 \tfrac12 z^{\mathsf T}Mz+q^{\mathsf T}z
 \quad\text{over }z\ge0.
\]
For a nonsymmetric matrix, however, the gradient of that quadratic expression is
$\tfrac12(M+M^{\mathsf T})z+q$, not $Mz+q$. Replacing $M$ by its symmetric part changes the problem.

Nor must that symmetric part be positive definite for a $P$-matrix. For
\[
 M=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\]
all principal minors are positive, but with $v=(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}$ one has $v^{\mathsf T}Mv=-1$. This matrix is easily solved by the triangular algorithm, yet the proposed general convex minimization argument has lost its hypothesis. A solvable subclass need not satisfy the additional structure used by another method.

\paragraph{A four-cycle in simultaneous coordinate updates.}
Consider the promised instance
\[
 M=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\-2&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad q=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The principal minors are $1,1,5$, so $M$ is a $P$-matrix. Its solution is $z=(1,1)$, $w=(0,0)$.

The tempting simultaneous update, solving each coordinate against the previous iterate, is
\[
 T(z_1,z_2)=\bigl(\max(0,3-2z_2),\max(0,-1+2z_1)\bigr).
\]
Starting from zero gives
\[
 (0,0)\mapsto(3,0)\mapsto(3,5)\mapsto(0,5)\mapsto(0,0).
\]
Thus this iteration never reaches the unique solution. Every iterate is nonnegative, but nonnegativity and uniqueness do not imply convergence. This is a counterexample to this particular simultaneous method, not to all pivot algorithms or to polynomial-time solvability. Changing update order, damping, or the search rule would require a fresh correctness and complexity argument.

\paragraph{Verification and outcome.}
Exact rational tests enumerate supports on small promised matrices, verify the triangular recurrence, and check every step of the displayed cycle. The determinant bounds and denominator accounting are symbolic; small numerical residuals are not used to certify complementarity.

\textbf{UNRESOLVED.} Polynomial solution encoding length, an exhaustive support algorithm, and the triangular polynomial-bit-time subcase are established. The first missing step is a deterministic polynomial-time method selecting a valid support for a general rational $P$-matrix, with no symmetry or triangularity assumption.

\subsection{Sources}
\begin{itemize}
\item[S1]A new combinatorial property of geometric unique sink orientations.
\url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.08992}.
\textit{Formulation source.}
\end{itemize}
